digest.title: Material Intelligence — 16 November 2026
digest.description: A weekly digest of AI methods and applications in materials science, based only on the supplied records.
digest.overview: This week’s preprints report progress in adapting and scaling atomistic models, steering crystal generation, extracting superconductivity data, and reconstructing nanoscale chemical maps. These are computational or methods results; proposed materials and workflows should not be mistaken for independently confirmed discoveries. The supplied excerpts are abstracts, not full papers.

stories.title: Fine-tuning an atomistic foundation model for sodium–carbon chemistry
stories.summary: A preprint reports that evaluated pretrained MACE foundation models do not accurately capture Na–Na and Na–C interactions for metallic sodium clusters on graphene. Targeted fine-tuning improved energetic descriptions and transfer to unseen Na/C environments. The authors use the resulting model to relate hard-carbon closed-pore radius to sodium-storage plateau voltage.
stories.whyItMatters: The work illustrates how targeted adaptation may make general-purpose atomistic models more useful for battery materials with competing bonding environments, and links local structure to a design-relevant property.
stories.limitation: This is a preprint available here only as an abstract. The pore-size/voltage relationship is a model-based finding; the supplied evidence does not establish experimental confirmation or broad transferability beyond the tested Na/C environments.

sources.title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
sources.evidence: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

stories.title: Inference-time search steers crystal generative models toward multiple goals
stories.summary: A preprint introduces Diffusion Tree Sampling, a Monte Carlo tree-search method that adapts crystal diffusion models at inference time without modifying their weights. The authors report improved stability in generated crystals, sampling for rare space groups and high bulk modulus, and multi-objective generation along a Pareto front for dielectric constant and band gap.
stories.whyItMatters: Inference-time adaptation could let one generative model serve different discovery objectives without a separate fine-tuning run for each task. Pareto-front sampling also makes trade-offs between target properties explicit.
stories.limitation: These are computational generation results in a preprint, not experimental syntheses or validation of generated materials. The supplied abstract does not establish how reliably the gains transfer to other models, objectives, or experimental conditions.

sources.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
sources.evidence: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

stories.title: A general-purpose agent connects materials data to proposed experiments
stories.summary: A preprint gives a language-model agent access to the authors’ Alexandria database, trained models, and reaction graph. The abstract reports unattended screening for a solar absorber, rejection of a candidate based on synthesis energetics, and preparation of a synthesis plan. For Ba–Zr–S, the agent proposes an unreported sulfide and an experiment intended to test it.
stories.whyItMatters: Connecting databases, property models, and reaction information in one workflow could help translate materials questions into testable experimental plans, rather than producing candidate lists alone.
stories.limitation: The sulfide and synthesis plans are proposals, not experimentally confirmed discoveries. The evidence is an abstract-only preprint and does not establish independent validation, general reliability, or how often the agent’s recommendations succeed in a laboratory.

sources.title: Materials research with a general-purpose agent
sources.evidence: Over the last decade we have built Alexandria, an open database of about 15 million density-functional calculations of crystals. It includes PBE, PBEsol, SCAN and TB-mBJ results, structures relaxed at pressures up to 150 GPa, dielectric tensors and about 145,000 electron-phonon calculations, together with more than 400 million structures relaxed with machine-learned potentials. On these data we trained a generative model for crystal structures, a universal interatomic potential and graph neural networks for more than ten properties, from band gaps to superconducting critical temperatures. From the convex hull we computed a reaction graph of the 17.4 billion reactions between its 193,416 stable compounds. Here we give all of this to a general-purpose language-model agent. Working unattended, the agent screens the database for a solar absorber, drops a candidate whose synthesis releases too little energy, and writes a synthesis plan with precursors, crucible and atmosphere. Asked about the well-studied Ba-Zr-S system, it finds an unreported sulfide and designs the experiment that would confirm or rule it out. Asked for an air-stable alternative, it designs one and tests it against new structures from the generative model. With web search alone, the same agent proposes what the literature already discusses. Put together, the data, the models and the reaction graph let a general agent do what none of them does alone: go from a question in plain words to an experiment that a laboratory can run and test.

stories.title: Distilled atomistic models enable large semiconductor-interface simulations
stories.summary: A preprint reports distilling a pretrained atomistic foundation model into compact ACE and NEP potentials for semiconductor interfaces. For simulations of systems up to 79,920 atoms, the authors report close agreement with DFT-trained counterparts on selected thermal and mechanical properties, while improving simulation speed and accessible system size by several orders of magnitude.
stories.whyItMatters: If these results generalize, distillation could make large-scale molecular dynamics of heterogeneous interfaces more practical while retaining useful responses from a much larger teacher model.
stories.limitation: The reported agreements apply to specific materials, properties, and tested configurations; the abstract notes that committee-based data selection did not consistently improve downstream properties. This is a preprint, and the results do not establish reliability for arbitrary interfaces or conditions.

sources.title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
sources.evidence: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

stories.title: Neural-process model reconstructs AFM-IR chemical maps from sparse spectra
stories.summary: A preprint presents a convolutional-attentive conditional neural process for reconstructing AFM-IR hyperspectral cubes from sparse measurements. The model was trained on synthetic cubes generated from experimental infrared spectra; on experimental polymer-particle datasets, the authors report competitive reconstruction using 5% of available spectra and uncertainty estimates for predicted intensities.
stories.whyItMatters: Reducing the number of spectra required could speed nanoscale chemical imaging, while uncertainty estimates may help direct measurements toward regions where further sampling is useful.
stories.limitation: Validation covers the supplied PMMA and polystyrene-in-epoxy datasets, and training uses synthetic cubes. The abstract does not establish performance across other materials, instruments, or sampling schemes, or demonstrate an autonomous sampling workflow experimentally.

sources.title: Uncertainty Aware AFM-IR Hyperspectral Cube Reconstruction via Convolutional-Attentive Conditional Neural Processes
sources.evidence: Atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) maps chemical composition at nanoscale spatial resolution, but the time required to acquire individual spectra limits hyperspectral imaging. Here, we introduce a convolutional-attentive conditional neural process (CACNP), a neural process architecture for reconstructing AFM-IR hyperspectral cubes from sparsely sampled spectra and a small set of structure images, each acquired at a selected wavenumber. The model is trained entirely on synthetic cubes generated from experimental infrared spectra and predicts both spectral intensities and their associated uncertainty. Validation on experimental datasets of poly(methyl methacrylate) and polystyrene particles embedded in epoxy demonstrates accurate reconstruction using only 5% of the available spectra, with competitive performance when compared to other methods. Inference takes less than 0.1 s on 128 X 128 hyperspectral cubes, supporting rapid reconstruction updates, while predictive uncertainty provides a basis for adaptive sampling of localized chemical features. This approach advances autonomous, high-throughput AFM-IR workflows and offers an architecture for accelerating other hyperspectral imaging methods.

stories.title: AutoSuperCon assembles experimental superconducting parameters from papers
stories.summary: A preprint introduces AutoSuperCon, a database of eight superconducting parameters with 20,354 entries for 6,793 superconductors, extracted from more than 47,000 arXiv preprints using a large language model. The authors report validation against reference data and train composition-based predictors for critical temperature and upper critical field.
stories.whyItMatters: A broader collection of experimental parameters could support materials analysis beyond critical-temperature prediction and provide a resource for screening known superconducting families.
stories.limitation: The database and reported predictors are presented in a preprint. Extraction from papers can inherit reporting and coverage biases; the abstract’s validation statistic does not establish correctness for every entry or predictive performance for new material families.

sources.title: Machine-accelerated extraction of experimental superconducting parameters for physical insight and prediction across thousands of materials
sources.evidence: New superconductors could unlock next-generation technologies from nuclear fusion to lossless electronics. Machine learning can predict candidate superconductors but lacks validated experimental training data beyond the critical temperature. Here we present AutoSuperCon, a database of eight superconducting parameters, containing 20354 entries for 6793 superconductors. The data were extracted from over 47000 arXiv preprints using a large language model and validated against reference datasets ($R^2 = 0.96$ with NIMS SuperCon). Using AutoSuperCon, we show that median gap ratios rise from 3.6 in conventional superconductors to 6.4 in cuprates, 28% of upper critical fields exceed the Pauli limit, and critical temperatures lie below a ceiling proportional to the superfluid density. Further, we train composition-based predictors for the critical temperature ($R^2_{\log}=0.83$) and the upper critical field ($R^2_{\log}=0.69$), boosted by transfer learning. Within known superconducting families, composition alone is sufficient to screen candidates for both parameters. AutoSuperCon thus enables physical insight and data-driven discovery across thousands of superconductors.

coverageGaps: Discovery is limited to curated arXiv and GitHub sources; excerpts are not full papers. arXiv retrieval is capped at 100 results; GitHub release feeds at 30. Broader web coverage is not included.

The predicted density is then used within the full-relativistic FP-TB-MTO framework combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function method. By combining first-principles accuracy with linear-scaling inference, DeltaChargeNet enables large-scale device simulations without the full DFT self-consistent field loop."},{"title":"A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18041v1","publishedAt":"2026-11-13","type":"Preprint","access":"Abstract only","evidence":"One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials."},{"title":"CGTransformer: A Topology-Aware Autoregressive Framework for Crystal Generation and Inverse Design","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18303v1","publishedAt":"2026-11-13","type":"Preprint","access":"Abstract only","evidence":"Autoregressive language models offer a unified route to crystal generation and inverse design, but their performance depends on how periodic structures are serialized. Symmetry equivalent and closely related crystals can receive different atomic orders under coordinate-based serialization, introducing variability unrelated to their structural connectivity. Here, we present CGTransformer (Crystal Graph Transformer), an autoregressive generative framework that addresses this challenge via a graph-embedded sorting strategy. Using quotientgraph topology and barycentric embeddings, Element Symmetry Graph (ESG) converts periodic crystal networks into topology-guided one-dimensional sequences that retain key local and symmetry-related structural information. CGTransformer achieves high generation validity and the highest single shot crystal structure prediction (CSP) match rate among the compared MP-20 baselines (63.24%), while same backbone comparisons show improved structure recovery over coordinate-based ordering. Furthermore, we demonstrate property-conditioned inverse design for wide-bandgap semiconductors, where ESG achieves a much higher stable, unique and novel (S.U.N.) rate and stronger target-property alignment than the coordinate-based baseline. These results establish topology-guided sequence construction as an effective route to improving crystal generation and property-directed design at fixed model capacity."},{"title":"Electric Fields Turn Vacancy-trapping Grain Boundaries into Li-Ion Pathways in Li2O","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17679v1","publishedAt":"2026-11-13","type":"Preprint","access":"Abstract only","evidence":"Ion transport in solids has conventionally been understood from equilibrium diffusion, yet ions in batteries are driven by electric fields. Does field-driven ion transport follow equilibrium behavior? We examined this question in bulk Li2O and at its grain boundaries (GBs) using electric-field molecular dynamics combining a machine learning interatomic potential with a Bader charge prediction model.
